question: Why must error-handling middleware in Express have exactly 4 arguments (err, req, res, next)?

options.text: Without the 4th argument next() will not work
options.explanation: next() works fine in regular middleware with 3 arguments. Express uses the argument count (4) as a signal that this is error-handling middleware

options.text: TypeScript requires 4 arguments for error typing
options.explanation: This is Express behavior, not TypeScript. Express checks function.length (number of parameters) -- if it is 4, this is error middleware

options.text: This is a convention that can be broken without consequences
options.explanation: This is not just a convention -- Express literally checks fn.length === 4 to determine error middleware. If the count is not 4, Express will not pass the error to this middleware

options.text: Express determines the middleware type by the number of arguments -- 4 arguments mean an error handler

question: What happens if an Express async handler throws an error without asyncHandler?

options.text: Node.js terminates the process with exit code 1
options.explanation: In newer Node.js versions unhandled rejections emit a warning but do not terminate the process by default. The problem is that the client receives no response and the error does not reach error middleware

options.text: An unhandled promise rejection occurs -- the error does not reach error middleware, and the client gets a hung request
Express automatically catches the error and passes it to error middleware
options.explanation: Express (before v5) does not intercept rejected promises from async handlers. The error becomes an unhandled rejection and the client receives no response

options.text: The client receives a 500 Internal Server Error response
options.explanation: Without asyncHandler Express is unaware of the error and cannot send a 500. The client simply receives no response -- the request hangs until timeout

question: In what order should middleware be connected in an Express application?

options.text: Order does not matter -- Express automatically optimizes the chain
options.explanation: Order is critical! Express executes middleware strictly in the order it was connected via app.use(). Incorrect order leads to bugs (undefined body, missing CORS, etc.)

options.text: Parsers (json, urlencoded) -> CORS -> logging -> authentication -> routes -> error handler
Error handler -> parsers -> CORS -> routes -> logging
options.explanation: The error handler must be last -- it handles errors from all preceding middleware and routes. If placed first, it catches nothing

options.text: Routes -> CORS -> parsers -> logging -> error handler
options.explanation: Routes must come after parsers and middleware, otherwise req.body is undefined, CORS headers are not set, and logging does not work

question: How does express.Router() differ from defining routes directly via app.get()?

options.text: Router is a mini-application for modular route organization with a shared prefix via app.use('/prefix', router)
Router is faster because it uses an optimized lookup algorithm
options.explanation: Performance is identical -- Router uses the same routing mechanism. Its advantage is modularity: routes can be moved to separate files and mounted with a prefix

options.text: Router supports middleware while app.get() does not
options.explanation: Both Router and app support middleware. The difference is modularity: Router allows grouping routes and mounting them as a plugin with a shared prefix

options.text: Router is only needed for TypeScript route typing
options.explanation: Router is not related to TypeScript -- it is a modular Express mechanism. It allows extracting route groups into separate files and mounting them with a prefix

question: What scopes can middleware have in Express?

options.text: On a specific route: app.get('/path', middleware, handler)
At the file level: middleware is applied to all routes in the file automatically
options.explanation: Express has no file-level scope for middleware. Scope is determined only by app.use() and its first argument (path), not by file structure

options.text: Global: app.use(middleware) -- applies to all routes
On a route group: app.use('/api', middleware) -- only for paths starting with /api
